reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it actively presents Mirror Trading International signup and team recruitment through referral links and placement options, including an invitation to join the speaker's team. It instructs viewers to send funds to a wallet, enter a Bitcoin amount and transaction ID, upload proof of payment, and transfer the amount into a trading pool. It also describes trading-bonus payments and compounding them back into the pool, although the supplied material does not independently verify payments, establish a guarantee, or show a completed withdrawal or loss.

opening.argument: Judge the speaker's claims by their limits. He describes moving funds into the trading pool as his own experience, saying, “So that's how it happened for me,” rather than promising that every viewer will profit. He also urges viewers to watch the tutorials to understand the platform. The walkthrough contains no stated guaranteed return, and the described trading-bonus screen does not itself prove a future payment to anyone. This is an account of how he uses the back office, not a substantiated promise of investment returns.

citations.quote: So that's how it happened for me and that's how it's done.
make sure you watch the video tutorials on all of these because then you could understand the whole back office

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited referral link and funding steps show what the interface permits; they do not establish a guaranteed return or prove that the speaker misrepresented a completed payout. Even his account of entering the pool is expressly tied to his own experience. Treat the payment and compounding language as claims requiring scrutiny, not independent proof that viewers were promised a particular result.

citations.quote: So that's how it happened for me and that's how it's done.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A guarantee is not necessary to recognize the pitch. The speaker gives viewers the steps to send funds and enter the trading pool, then describes getting paid and compounding those amounts. Calling the process his own experience does not remove the invitation to participate or the return-oriented framing.

opening.argument: The video's immediate task is operational: it shows the phone version of a back office, explains where registration links appear, and walks through the fields used when adding funds. The speaker also directs viewers to the site's video tutorials so they can understand the back office. A judge should distinguish demonstrating an interface from verifying the platform's claims: the walkthrough tells viewers where controls are, but it does not independently establish that trading profits or withdrawals occur.

citations.quote: I'm here on my Android phone pretty much showing you guys from this version, instead of the computer.
enter amount sent, then you want to also paste the transaction.
just watch the videos get it out the way and then you will have a better understanding of what's going on

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening accurately identifies referral, funding, and pool controls, but those are precisely the controls an operational walkthrough would cover. Its quoted payment language describes where a report appears; neither that report nor the tutorial independently verifies a paid return. The evidence therefore supports reading this primarily as instruction about an interface.

citations.quote: you pretty much go here where it's a trading bonus report

true_side_reply.rebuttal: This is more than neutral interface instruction. The speaker tells viewers how to send funds, says transferring them to the pool is how they trade Bitcoin on the platform, and presents trading-bonus payments as something they will see. The tutorial format is the vehicle for promoting participation in the pool.

citations.quote: with that address that's where you would send your funds to

when you start getting paid you pretty much go here where it's a trading bonus report

opening.argument: The referral material can be read as ordinary team promotion: the speaker explains registration and website links, discusses where a new member can be placed, and invites a prospective builder to contact him before joining. That does not, by itself, show that recruits receive downline income or that the speaker is asking for their credentials. The funding form asks for a transaction ID and proof of payment, while the supplied walkthrough shows no completed withdrawal or independently verified return. Those gaps matter before treating every referral and account-funding instruction as evidence of deception.

citations.quote: You've got two different referral links that you can use. You can use the Registration link or the Website link.

put that ID in there and then right here say choose a file to show the picture that it's on its way

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening shows a referral workflow and a deposit workflow, but its quotes do not establish downline compensation, a guaranteed return, or a completed investor payout. The speaker's invitation to talk before joining also leaves room for a personal referral reading. The judge should not fill those missing facts in merely because the interface has team-placement and trading-pool features.

citations.quote: Let's talk before you even join.
and then that's when you send your amount.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern does not depend on proving downline compensation or credential theft. The speaker recruits for his team, directs viewers to send funds and transfer them into a trading pool, then describes trading-bonus payments being compounded there. That combination makes the referral and funding instructions part of an investment-pool promotion, regardless of whether a withdrawal is shown.
